claim: Ceratopsid dental systems are among the most specialized structures in Dinosauria by the presence of tooth batteries and high-angled wear surfaces.
source: The dental system of ceratopsids is among the most specialized structure in Dinosauria by the presence of tooth batteries and high-angled wear surfaces.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as a characterization of ceratopsid dental systems, drawing on established knowledge about these dinosaurs.

claim: The origin of the ceratopsid dental system is poorly understood due to a lack of relevant knowledge in early-diverging ceratopsians.
source: However, the origin of this unique dental system is poorly understood due to a lack of relevant knowledge in early-diverging ceratopsians.
evidence: This statement identifies a gap in scientific knowledge about early ceratopsian dental evolution.

claim: Chaoyangsaurus is from the Late Jurassic of Liaoning Province.
source: Chaoyangsaurus from the Late Jurassic of Liaoning Province
evidence: This is a factual statement about the temporal and geographic origin of this specimen.

claim: Early-diverging ceratopsians have no more than five replacement teeth in each jaw quadrant.
source: no more than five replacement teeth in each jaw quadrant
evidence: This finding is based on micro-CT analysis of the three studied specimens.

claim: Early-diverging ceratopsians have at most one replacement tooth in each alveolus.
source: at most one replacement tooth in each alveolus
evidence: This finding is based on micro-CT analysis of the three studied specimens.

claim: Early-diverging ceratopsians show nearly full resorption of the functional tooth root.
source: nearly full resorption of the functional tooth root
evidence: This finding is based on micro-CT analysis of the three studied specimens.

claim: Early-diverging ceratopsians have occlusion with low-angled, concave wear facets.
source: occlusion with low-angled, concave wear facets
evidence: This finding is based on micro-CT analysis of the three studied specimens.

claim: Yinlong displays an increase in the number of maxillary alveoli during ontogeny.
source: Yinlong displays an increase in the number of maxillary alveoli and a decrease in the number of replacement teeth during ontogeny
evidence: This is based on comparison of specimens of different sizes representing different ontogenetic stages.

claim: Yinlong displays a decrease in the number of replacement teeth during ontogeny.
source: Yinlong displays an increase in the number of maxillary alveoli and a decrease in the number of replacement teeth during ontogeny
evidence: This is based on comparison of specimens of different sizes representing different ontogenetic stages.

claim: The largest individual of Yinlong retains functional tooth remnants.
source: as well as the retention of functional tooth remnants in the largest individual
evidence: This is based on CT analysis of specimen IVPP V18637.

claim: Chaoyangsaurus and Hualianceratops have slightly more replacement teeth than Yinlong.
source: Chaoyangsaurus and Hualianceratops have slightly more replacement teeth than Yinlong.
evidence: This is based on comparative analysis of CT data from the three taxa.

claim: Early-diverging ceratopsians display a relatively slow tooth replacement rate.
source: In general, early-diverging ceratopsians display a relatively slow tooth replacement rate
evidence: This is inferred from the low number of replacement teeth observed in the specimens.

claim: Early-diverging ceratopsians likely use gastroliths to triturate foodstuffs.
source: and likely use gastroliths to triturate foodstuffs
evidence: This is inferred from the slow tooth replacement rate and the presence of gastroliths in some specimens.

claim: The difference in dietary strategy might have influenced the tooth replacement pattern in later-diverging ceratopsians.
source: The difference in dietary strategy might have influenced the tooth replacement pattern in later-diverging ceratopsians.
evidence: This is a speculative statement about evolutionary relationships between diet and tooth replacement.

claim: Ceratopsids developed dental batteries composed of a large number of teeth that interlocked vertically and rostrocaudally in the jaw.
source: During the Cretaceous, the ceratopsids became one of the dominant herbivorous terrestrial clades and developed dental batteries composed of a large number of teeth that interlocked vertically and rostrocaudally in the jaw (Edmund, 1960; Dodson et al., 2004).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research on ceratopsid dentition.

claim: Ceratopsids developed two-rooted teeth to facilitate vertical integration of the tooth batteries with up to 5 teeth in each vertical series.
source: Ceratopsids developed two-rooted teeth to facilitate vertical integration of the tooth batteries with up to 5 teeth in each vertical series (Edmund, 1960).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Edmund 1960.

claim: Protoceratops retains single-rooted teeth which have no more than 2 replacement teeth in each alveolus.
source: This contrasts with nonceratopsid taxa such as Protoceratops which retain single-rooted teeth which, although compacted rostrocaudally, have no more than 2 replacement teeth in each alveolus (Edmund, 1960).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Edmund 1960.

claim: Early Cretaceous neoceratopsians, including Auroraceratops and Archaeoceratops, have only 1 replacement tooth in each alveolus.
source: The Early Cretaceous neoceratopsians, including Auroraceratops and Archaeoceratops, have only 1 replacement tooth in each alveolus (Tanoue et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Tanoue et al. 2012.

claim: Liaoceratops has 2 replacement teeth per alveolus and shallow sulci on the roots to facilitate close-packing.
source: By using computed tomography, He et al., 2018 added more detailed information on the Early Cretaceous neoceratopsian Liaoceratops and presented evidence of the presence of the 2 replacement teeth per alveolus and shallow sulci on the roots to facilitate close-packing.
evidence: This is supported by citation to He et al. 2018.

claim: Tracts of partially resorbed functional teeth in Liaoceratops appear to follow the growth of the jaws.
source: Tracts of partially resorbed functional teeth in Liaoceratops appear to follow the growth of the jaws.
evidence: This is based on observations from He et al. 2018.

claim: Liaoceratops represents the first amniote for which multiple generations of tooth remnants are documented.
source: Liaoceratops represents the first amniote for which multiple generations of tooth remnants are documented (He et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citation to He et al. 2018.
